Presidential RamblingsBy Steve Hansen
It was a truly engaging and insightful demo/talk by
Art Liestman last month as he challenged us to
sharpen our eye through his playful discussion of
both natural egg shapes and turned egg shapes
(donated by our members) - a most innovative approach for inciting discussion on shape, form, and
tuning our perspective of shape and pleasant line.
It was great to see and hear so many people actively participate in this demo. As one of our founding
members and the guiding light during our early
years, Art brings a wealth of experience in his approach to creativity – thank you Art!
From last month’s outstanding newsletter this
stood out for me: “What before was hard became
easier and what seemed impossible became doable.” These words of enlightenment from Bruce
Campbell reflect two important things. You will encounter problems and with perseverance you will
overcome them.
I dropped in on the latest Turning 101 class. Lo and
behold there were six fully engaged student turners and four volunteers on hand supporting their
endeavour. The highly skilled Claudia Hayward was
heading the class with instruction, along with the
helping hands of John Hammond, Keith Ruttan, and
Brian Lunt. Out of sight but equally important are
Peter Hill, our T101 co-ordinator, and Dan Breck,
our resident wood hound and bee charmer who
collected the wood, along with Brian, to provide
our students with plenty of wood to make shavings. WOW, what a team effort!
One final note, in one of our recent Zoom chats
there was considerable talk about finishes for table
ware. What looks good to sell? What is easy to
maintain by the customer? With that in mind I
thought Mike Mahoney’s talk about bowl finishes
might shed some light on the topic: https://
www.youtube.com/watch?v=ITYyrYLgEfI – hope
this helps!
Steve

Editor’s NotesBy Steve Fairbairn
We have a larger than usual newsletter this month,
kicking off with our always informative Tech Talk.
Also returning, a GVWG member profile featuring
Marco Berera, probably one of most skilled, and
humble, makers it’s been my pleasure to know.
Sheila Balzer continues to chronical her journey as
an artist and relatively new woodturner.
This month’s cover photo is a scale model of the
Saturn V rocket made by Fraser MacLean who has
written a very detailed and wonderfully illustrated
article about its construction. Dex Hallwood has
written an informative article on his experience
rebuilding a chuck.
Bruce Campbell has written a detailed report on
the recent Focus On Fundamentals presentation
and Claudia Hayward reports on the recent Turning
101 sessions along with a number of photos.
However, large size of this month’s newsletter is
due, in most part, by the wonderfully large number
of Gallery entries in January.
Thanks to all who contributed articles for the newsletter and hope to see more articles about your
projects, tool hacks or other musings.
Steve

Tech TalkBy Bruce Campbell
The First Tech Talk ZOOM session of 2023 was held
at 7:00PM on Monday January 30th – the Monday
after our Guild meeting. As usual, the discussion
was varied and prompted lots of follow-on
thoughts.
Members sometimes give me feedback of things
they heard at our session while others contact me
outside the session to share things they think fit
within Tech Talk. I am happy to say that both
those things have happened last month.
Making Small Diameter Dowels
Making small (under ¼”) and uniform dowels by
hand is possible but takes a lot of practice. However, I learned a fast, easy, and very accurate easy
way to do it using a metal drill index card.
1. Mount your stock in a chuck and turning the
free end round and down to somewhere close
to the size you want and with a small point on
the end.
2. Remove the live center from your tailstock and
bring it up close to the work.
3. Select a hole in you index card that is just a
little smaller than the roughed out piece and
slip it over the point of the piece.
4. Using the quill and push the index card the
whole length of the piece.
5. Retract the quill and card together. This helps
to keep the card square to the work.
6. Select the next smallest size hole on the index
card and repeat steps 3, 4, and 5.
7. Repeat this until you reach the diameter you
want.
The holes in the index card are punched from one
side (usually the side with the sizes marked on it).
The edges of the holes on that side are slightly
rounded over while they are square on the other
side. Be sure to have the square-edge side toward
the work and the rounded-edge side to the tailstock.
Click HERE to see a short video of this technique.
Fraser was very excited to see the dowel making
trick and immediately set to work making a shaft
from the propeller for one of his model planes. It is
really rewarding when our tech Talk has such an
immediate and positive impact to our membership.
(Continued on page 5)
Tech Talk is held on the Monday evening following
the Guild ZOOM session. The credentials for the
session are sent to all registered Guild members
and all are encouraged to participate in the freeflowing discussion centered on technical aspects of
woodturning.

A Story Stick Comb
Fraser found a simple way to make a story stick using an ordinary plastic comb. He purchased as set
from a Dollar Store and found they all had different
tooth spacing which worked to his advantage. To
make a story stick he selects a comb with the right
spacing and clips of those teeth he doesn’t need
leaving the ones he wants proud. He even leaves
to first heavy tooth as a stop to position the comb
for marking his piece.
Cleaning and Lubricating a 4-jaw Chuck
Ross was not able to be at the meeting but contacted me directly both for advice and to follow up
on his success. He had found that his chuck had
become very hard to open and close.
My first suggestion was to give it a good blow with
compressed air focusing on the jaw carriers and
the back where the scroll plate is exposed. Then
spray a good dose of WD40 (or equivalent – see
https://www.primalsurvivor.net/wd-40-substitute )
and let it sit a minute before blasting it again with
compressed air. Finally, spray the guides and scroll
with a good-quality spray lubricant.
If you are still not happy with the result remove the
scroll disc (you will need to remove the large snap
ring to do this) and give both it and the back area
of the chuck body a thorough cleaning. Also check
for damage or wear of the scroll threads themselves. If they are damaged you may need to file
them smooth and in rare cases replace it. I have
encountered several cases where longer jaw
screws were used on a Vicmarc chuck which fouled
and actually broke part of the scroll disc.
There are a few videos on Youtube that go through
how to do this and I recommend you look them up
if you have to go beyond the basic cleaning and
lubricating.
Thanks for sending this in, Ross.
Editor’s Note: See the next article in this newsletter
for further guidance on rebuilding chucks.
Safe Disposal of Boeshield T-9
Bob asked about disposing of Boeshield T-9 – an
industrial waterproof lubricant and corrosion protector. Several people shared that it is a very safe
product and can be taken to a municipal disposal
site.
This started a wider discussion about disposing of
unwanted spray and liquid products. In general, if
it is a drying product like paint just allow it to dry
before taking it to a municipal disposal site. If it is
a spray product that dries then simply spray it to
exhaustion on a disposable surface (like cardboard)
(Continued from page 4)
(Continued on page 6)
Story stick comb

February 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 6
and then dispose of the empty can and cardboard.
We are in a rare position to work with one of Nature’s truly wonderful products – wood. In return,
we need to take care of the environment by choosing environmentally safe products, using our materials wisely and disposing of things safely.
Squeaky Belts
David reported that the belt on his lathe makes a
squeaking sound until it is warmed up and wondered how to address the problem. Several people
suggested spray belt treatments but Dave reported
that he tried some of those and had little success.
Another suggestion was that cold could be causing
the problem. Dave confirmed that he works in an
unheated shop and that he would try turning on
the radiator a while before he starts turning.
High Tech Depth Measurer
Michael shared his high-tech system to measure
the exact thickness of the bottom of his bowls. He
writes:
As a relatively new turner I've certainly experienced the "joy" of going a bit too deep a number of
times when cutting the inside of a bowl.
In most cases my simple homemade depth gauge
works fine and guides me when I "eyeball" the
thickness of the bottom. However, when doing a
very thin walled bowls I found eyeballing is not accurate enough.
I bought a laser distance meter for $30 from Amazon and mounted it on a platform at the end of my
lathe in a way that it is easy to put on and remove
and will ALWAYS be in the exact same spot. I had
previously built a homemade lathe extension so I
have a little slot where I mount a metal plate and
that locks the platform in place. Otherwise I would
gerry-rig some other solution; perhaps using welding magnets or drilling dog-pin holes in the ways.
(Continued from page 5)
(Continued on page 7)
Digital depth measuring device

February 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 7
Once the unit is set in place I measured the distance to the FRONT of the jaws and use that measurement to calculate the EXACT thickness of the
bottom of my thin bowls.
Not all chuck/jaw combinations are the same so I
have done the calculations for each setup and
made a handy reference chart.
Thanks for sharing this, Michael, and may all your
future bowls have complete bottoms.
Restoring a Damaged Morse Taper
Steve H shared how he fixed a damaged Morse Taper. He writes:
Below is a picture showing the remnants of damage to my Jacobs Check MT after it spun in the
headstock (many years ago). The male MT has
since been honed with a diamond file but the female side was more difficult to fix.
I wrapped 320 grit adhesive-backed sandpaper onto the MT making sure not to overlap the paper
and then used that to ream the female portion
smooth. This process seems to have worked well as
the MT mating is now very smooth and effective. I
also added a grub screw by tapping into the quill
and employ this feature when drilling deeply or
using large bits.
DIY Fresh Air Respirator
Steve H does not like using dust masks mostly because they cause his glasses to fog up. He has been
thinking of a way to breathe clean air in a dusty
environment and shared his most recent DIY project us. He writes:
In addition to my room filter and a localised dust
sucker, I use a CPAP machine mounted at the ceiling to supply myself with fresh air. Basically it is a
VERY expensive fan! The air supply is via a 3 foot
articulating arm which rides on a support beam
and attaches to a flex-hose and then the headset.
In addition, I have attached two retracting lanyards
along the hose to help keep it out the way.
For the intake, the air is drawn from another room
in the house (note a rubber hose to the right of the
machine at ceiling level) and is currently not employing a filter. To balance the air pressure from
one room to another I rely on the quality of a leaky
(Continued from page 6)
(Continued on page 8)

DYI Heat Treating Furnace
Fraser recently had success in making a tri-point
beading tool from mild steel and then tempering it
using a DYI heat treating furnace. He began by
making a CAD drawing of his setup and then purchased several fire-bricks for his build and used his
propane metalsmithing torch to the furnace.
He was very pleased with the setup and was able
to quickly heat the bar and quench temper it to a
nice hard tool.

Rebuilding a ChuckBy Dex Hallwood
Chucks are a workhorse when turning projects.
They are always being used but seldom thought
about. We might give them a wipe with a cloth
after use or blow them out with a blast of compressed air but over the years, even though they
are mostly sealed units, dirt and dust can get inside, lubrication deteriorates, and eventually the
jaws no longer open and close as smoothly as they
did when the chuck was new.
Recently I found my chucks more difficult to operate. They still worked well but seemed less smooth
and occasionally a bit catchy when I turned the
chuck key. Since I’m not mechanically inclined, I
assumed that taking apart a chuck to see what the
problem was would be well beyond my mechanical
ability. Never the less, curiosity got the better of
me and I Googled chuck maintenance and repair.
After looking at a few YouTube videos and checking
the chuck manufacturer’s website I was amazed at
how few moving parts the are in a chuck and how
few tools I needed to make the repair.
Basically the chuck consists of:
•
Chuck Body
•
Pinion Gears (2)
•
Backing Plate
•
Scroll Ring
•
Retaining Ring
•
Jaw Slides (4)
Tools or supplies required to disassemble and clean
the chuck:
•
Allen Key
•
Circlip Pliers
•
Plastic or Rubber Mallet
•
Wire brush / Toothbrush
•
WD40 or paint thinner to soak and clean the
parts
•
Lubricant (I used White Lithium Grease) before
reassembling
Because every chuck is a little different, I won’t go
through the steps as you will be able to find excellent directions on YouTube for your model of
chuck. The process is well worth it as once cleaned
and reassembled, your chuck will be like brand
new. I encourage you to try it as it is very simple
and straightforward to do.
Do remember to wear safety glasses when using
Circlip pliers as the snap ring can fly off in any direction if you are not careful.
Here is a photo of my Nova chuck after cleaning
and before reassembly:

This Month’s Cover
-Saturn V Apollo 11 1:144
Scale Model BuildBy Fraser MacLean
Why the Saturn V?
This space craft has always fascinated me since I
gave a presentation to the Cub Scout group in
1968. I had a Revell plastic model that I built and
used it to explain the sequence of events that
would lead to the moon landing. It would seem I’ve
had a desire to present technical information since
an early age.
I also belong to a solid wooden model building
group online that is a wealth of information on display model building from scratch. When the GVWG
Presidents challenge was themed “Celestial”, it revived my memory of the Saturn V and would be a
perfect two-fer of a project to build. Checkout the
members projects at:
http://smm.solidmodelmemories.net/SMF/
index.php
Researching the prototype
Looking for good drawings is always a challenge
and fun with the internet. There were several iterations of the Saturn V with differences in design details and paint schemes. I narrowed it down to the
Apollo 11 version, but even then, it seemed not
everyone agreed on what it looked like either.
So I settled on what appeared to be the correct
configuration for this model. The real rocket is
363+ feet high from the exhaust nozzles on the F1
engines to the top of the escape tower and is 33
feet in diameter. This scaled out using 1:144 to
30.25” high and 2.75” in diameter. Now, here’s an
interesting thing about the effect of scaling something to down to 1:144. The volume is reduced by
144 cubed. (144x144x144). The real rocket
weighed 6,000,000 pounds loaded with fuel. 144
cubed is approximately 3 million. The model
weighs 1.75 lb and when multiplied out is
5,250,000. So the density of the wooden model
rocket is only 7% less than the real rocket. In other
words the Saturn V was only slightly denser overall
than dry spruce.. But I digress….
Turning the first and second stages
I jointed the face of a nice straight grained spruce
2x4 then cut it to length to laminate into a 3x3
block. The intention was to make the 1st and 2nd
stages from the same section to get the diameters
consistent. I have a Laguna 12/16 lathe with the
short extension bed so it would just fit between
centers.
(Continued on page 12)

February 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 12
The first and second stages are separated by an
interstage skirt section of the same diameter. I was
able to turn a consistent diameter end to end using
only the roughing gouge. I squared the ends with
my table saw after turning and then using my calculated dimensions, cut the cylinder into the three
sections.
Not until I started to mask for the markings did I
discover the second stage was 1.75” too short. It
seems that I forgot to add the removed length of
the interstage skirt to the second stage. So after
my plan to avoid making separate cylinders, I now
had to remake the second stage. Undramatically,
the new second stage turned out well and matched
the skirt it was sitting on quite nicely.
The interstage skirt was then drilled hollow using a
forstner bit.
Turning the third stage with tapered interstage fairing
This tapered fairing was turned as a cone on the
lathe going from the diameter of the second stage
and reducing to the base diameter of the third
stage. It was held in a standard Nova chuck and the
taper was made with the small end towards the
chuck. The centre was also drilled out with a forstner bit and the wall thickness tapered with a bowl
gouge. The walls were left thicker than the scale
size to allow for the stages to be held together with
brass pins.
The third stage is much smaller in diameter and
was able to be turned from a 2x2 section of spruce.
It also has a long taper that is the fairing containing
the lunar module. Again all the turning to diameter
was with a roughing gouge with the taper finished
with a 3/8 gouge. The top end of the stage was
drilled off lathe to allow the command module engine nozzle to fit inside. Why was it drilled off
lathe? I forgot to make room for the command
module engine nozzle.
Command module and capsule
I decided to construct the command module and
capsule as a single turning. It’s quite small and they
remained together until just before re-entry to
Earth.
I actually turned this part first while I was waiting
for the laminations of the main rocket to setup.
(Continued from page 11)
(Continued on page 13)
First stage aft masking
Third stage aft end engine support

February 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 13
Plus it gave me a chance to practice turning the
cone to an actual angle as shown in the drawings I
had.
Launch escape system
This structure is composed of three parts on this
model: the rocket motor, tower structure and
shield.
The rocket motor was turned and was inspired by a
members construction of a golf tee in an earlier
challenge. It was turned from a 1/2” dowel held in
a collet. I have found the collets to be a great addition to making small detail parts.
The escape tower structure was fabricated
from .020” brass rod and fine wire. I made a fixture
to hold the pieces in place until the structure was
soldered together. The fine wire diagonals were
held in place by CA glue.
To make the launch shield covering the capsule, I
measured the actual size of the capsule to construct a cone from paper. Two cones were made
(cut on the silhouette) and bonded together with a
staggered joint. It was then coated with cyano clue
to harden it. It was at this point I glued my fingers
together enough that I spent ten minutes freeing
them apart with acetone.
During assembly, the components were held in
place with self closing tweezers mounted to stands
while they where glued.
F1 engine first stage fairings
There are four fairings at the base of the stage that
are turned from spruce. The fairing is not simply an
evenly split cone as it is more than 180 degrees of
arc at the bottom. So four cones had to be made
and split appropriately. The resulting flat surface
was carved out to fit the radius of the rocket and
(Continued from page 12)
(Continued on page 14)
Launch cover with command module & capsule
Escape tower rocket on the lathe
Escape tower assembly

February 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 14
they were fastened with wooden dowels and glue.
Once they were in place, the wood in the aft end of
the fairings was carved away using a Dremel tool to
leave a thin rim.
Rocket engines
There are five main engines on the first stage, five
on the second, one on the third and one on the
command module.
The larger F1 engines were turned in pairs between
centres and separated. I made a profile gauge from
styrene plastic using the silhouette vinyl cutter.
The styrene is more rigid than cardboard and
worked very well to keep them consistent. After
separating them, the small diameter section was
held by a collet while the inner material was removed from the nozzle. I did not cut the inside too
deep or thin as the weight of the model will be
supported by the engines. The actual rocket was
supported by four hard points to support the
weight or the engines would have been crushed
flat….
The six smaller J2 engines and the command module engine were turned from dowel held in the collet.
The F1 engines had additional parts made from
sections of pvc pipe and dowel held in place
by .020” brass pins and glue. All of the engines are
secured to the model with .062” brass pins.
Stage assembly pins
I use .062” brass pins set into corresponding .062”
id tubing glued into the model parts. I set the pins
first and used them to mark the locations of the
tubes for match drilling, similar to dowels.
Painting
I use high build automotive spray primer/filler in a
can for the first coats and sand as required. Automotive glazing putty is also used as a filler for joints
and surface defects. Once it is sanded smooth,
masking is accomplished using Tamiya model
masking tape for critical areas. Wide open areas
are masked with Washi tape (cheaper from Micheals) and tissue paper as needed.
(Continued from page 13)
(Continued on page 15)
F1 engine fairing cones
F1 engine turning sequence
Engine fairings pinned

February 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 15
After masking I airbrush the colours with Vallejo
Model Air paint. It is a really nice paint that covers
well and is very thin. Prior to painting with silver, I
spray the part black first as it gives the silver more
depth.
Markings
I used masks for the main lettering. The silhouette
is used to create the masks for spray painting. This
technique works on really fine paint details with
lines .020” wide being easily achieved. For the
flags and the fin marks, I used white printable vinyl
and a colour inkjet to get the detail for these small
items.
That just about covers the construction and building of this model. The lathe was central to building
it and allowed for very precise parts to be created.
Now my grandson wants his own rocket ship!
(Continued from page 14)

Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 16
The Focus on Fundamentals (FoF) ZOOM session
was held at 7:00PM on Thursday February 16th under the careful direction of Chris Stiles. FoF has
been suspended since the start of the pandemic
and Chris is working hard to revitalize it. Using the
success of Tech Talk, we have decided to do these
sessions over ZOOM so that more people can participate and to give more time for questions and
commentary.
Chris outlined what we can expect to see during
FoF over the next year. The target audience will be
beginner turners and each session will cover a single “fundamental” of woodturning. A selected presenter will give a short (20 mins) live or a prerecorded presentation on the chosen topic followed by question and discussion.
The topic for this session was using the Spindle
Roughing Gouge (SRG) and Chris chose himself to
be the presenter.
Presentation
Chris started by pointing out that a SRG is meant
exclusively for spindle turning and is very dangerous to use on cross-grain projects like bowls. This
is chiefly because the SRG has the largest cutting
edges of all our tools while also having one of the
smallest tangs. In cross-grain projects it is very
easy to suddenly get a very large bite of timber and
the instantaneous impact can easily overpower the
turners grip and rip the tool from their hands or
even break the tang.
Using pre-recorded videos Chris began talking
about how to find the proper bevel angle with a
SRG. He recommended anchoring the SRG to the
toolrest that has been set so the cutting edge rises
up to just above center. Roughing often starts by
cutting mostly air so finding the bevel edge can be
tricky. With the tool held at right angles to the
wood he recommends to drop the handle low
enough that as the tool is advanced into the piece
the back edge of the bevel (often called the heel)
hits first. Then by slowly raising the handle the
cutting edge will engage. At that moment the bevel is perfectly oriented to cut. Raising the handle
more will over-rotate the bevel and begin to scrape
the timber.
Start at the ends and cut outward working closer to
the center with each cut. As the high points are
removed you can speed up the lathe and take
deeper cuts. As wood is removed the gap between
the toolrest and wood will grow so remember to
stop the lathe and move the toolrest in once the
gap gets too large (1 to 2 inches).
Chris showed a simple trick for checking if the timber is round by lightly resting the back to the SRG
on the top of the piece. If the tool bounces the
piece still has some flat spots.
Once the piece is round Chris showed how to take
advantage of the flat wings of the SRG to make a
skewing cut. Roll and swing the tool until the bevel
of the inside wing is floating on the wood and then
slowly push the tool along the piece like a bowl or
spindle gouge. When the angle is just right the SRG
(Continued on page 17)
Focus On Fundamentals for February 2023
-
Using the Spindle Roughing GougeBy Bruce Campbell
Spindle Roughing Gouge Basic Setup

February 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 17
will cut very much like a skew leaving a smooth finish.
Next, he showed how by sharpening a short (1/2”)
section of the top edges of the flutes the SRG can
make a very good dressing tool that will allow you
to square up the end of the work and then by rolling the flute closed you can cut a tenon directly
with the SRG. By rolling the flute slightly more the
SRG will cut a dovetailed tenon.
Finally, Chris showed a brief video on how to
sharpen the SRG. The edge of an SRG should be
flat and square to the flute of the tool. Avoid having a dip in the center or having the wings swept
back from the nose.
It is important to have a grinder with a fully adjustable platform that allows you to set it such that the
current bevel angle of the tool matches the wheel.
An aid for doing this is to colour the current bevel
with a felt pen and then set if on the platform and
hand spin the grinder. Inspect here the ink has
been removed and adjust the platform until the
wheel removes all of the ink from edge to heel at
the same time.
When the platform is set and locked in position
switch on the grinder and lightly present the SRG
square to the wheel and roll it right and left to
grind the entire bevel. Be sure to keep the back of
the tool fully in contact with the platform and always square to the wheel. It only takes a few light
passes to restore an excellent edge to the tool.
Discussion
One attendee asked about the flute design on a
SRG and how that compared to a continental spindle gouge. Continental spindle gouges are a bar of
flat steel that is rolled lengthwise to form a shallow
flute. These are typically sharpened with a rounded edge much like a round-nosed scraper and can
have a bevel between 40 and 60 degrees. These
can be used to round spindles and have all the versatility of a spindle gouge but are often quite a bit
wider making them difficult to use for fine work.
Modern SRGs have a three-part design to their
flute. The wings are nearly straight and the central
section is round. This allows the SRG to perform
like a skew while still cutting the same way regardless of the section of the edge being used.
The topic of SRGs
made from round
stock with heavy
central tangs was
brought up. These
recent addition to
the
market
do
offer a much more
robust tang and
can be used with
interchangeable
handles
but
to
date the companies that offer these designs do not
grind their flutes to have the 3-section design mentioned above. Indeed, they are basically very large
“U” flute bowl gouges and, in the opinion of the
author, offer no advantage over a well-made SRG.
Many thanks to Chris for covering this topic so
well. It bodes well for FoF sessions in the future.

The first Turning 101 of the new year completed
last weekend. Six enthusiastic participants, Thalia
MacIssac, Norm King, Brian Andrews, David Rahn,

bright and early Saturday morning prepared to
make shavings. They all had some experience with
turning, all had access to lathes and were particularly keen to improve their toolwork and their confidence. We spent the first weekend turning green
wood blanks into bowls with brief discussions of
sharpening, dealing with green wood, sanding and

on the floor. The following Saturday gave an exposure to some spindle work including the skew,
roughing gouge and spindle gouge to make beads,
coves and v-grooves. They all came away realizing
that more practice and more practice is what is
necessary to improve ones’ woodturning.

woodturning. Many thanks to the gremlins who
supplied the wood, and particularly to Peter Hill for
stickhandling the organization, to Keith Ruttan and
John Hammond (my able assistants) and Brian Lunt

get into woodturning
When I completed my secondary education in Switzerland, it was time to start an apprenticeship. In
my home town of Brugg, there was a machine factory and I could start there as an apprentice
patternmaker (nothing to do with clothing) where I
worked for four years and attended Tech School for

practice pieces, but still full working patterns with
coreboxes (producing the interior of the casting).

Safety Guidelines for WoodturningYou mostly turn alone so safety is YOUR responsibility
 Always wear safety goggles or safety
glasses that include side protectors.
Use a full face shield for bowl, vessel, or
any turning involving chucks and faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/
or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder and
wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting
wrenches, and knockout bars immediately after use. Never leave them in
place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose
clothing, jewelry, or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating parts
or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the
workpiece is solidly mounted with stout
screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws
as a minimum). Do not use dry wall or
deck screws.
 When turning between centres, be certain the workpiece is firmly mounted
between the headstock driving centre
and tailstock centre.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in
place.
 Check that all locking devices on the
tailstock and tool rest assembly (rest
and base) are tight before operating the
lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by
hand to make sure it clears the toolrest
and bed before turning the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind
and in front of the workpiece, they are
the most likely areas for a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of this zone when
turning on the lathe, keeping your hand
on the switch in case you need to turn
the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning it on. Use slower speeds
for larger diameters or rough pieces
and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the
lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always
stop the machine to verify why. As a
starting point, consult your operator’s
manual for recommended speeds for a
particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed
is compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock
with cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets,
(Continued on page 56)

February 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 56
knots, irregular shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid these types
of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the
toolrest, holding the tool in a controlled
but comfortable manner. Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless it is securely
tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations.
An experienced woodturner is capable
of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning
turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before
sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing,
and keep your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check
for damaged parts, alignment, binding
of moving parts, and other conditions
that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better
and safer performance. Don’t force a
dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose
for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t
use a lathe in damp or wet locations.
Do not use in presence of flammable
liquids or gases, and always keep a fully
-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing.
Pay close attention to unusual sounds
or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate machines
when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect
electric cords for damage. Avoid the
use of extension cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn power off. Don’t leave
lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
 Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially band and
